claim: Abnormal spiral and scroll waves stimulate the heart to rapid, repetitive and inefficient contraction in a periodic manner in the case of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (mVT).
source: These abnormal waves stimulate the heart to rapid, repetitive and inefficient contraction, either in a periodic manner, as in the case of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (mVT) (Cysyk and Tung, 2008), or in a quasi-periodic to chaotic manner, as in the case of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (pVT) and fibrillation (Antzelevitch and Burashnikov, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The state-of-the-art technique for controlling the dynamics of abnormal waves involves global electrical synchronization achieved by applying high-voltage electric shocks to the heart.

evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Poor light penetration is considered a major limitation of optogenetics, as the applied supra-threshold illumination cannot be expected to affect sub-surface electrical activity in the heart wall.
source: This is considered a major limitation of optogenetics, as the applied supra-threshold illumination cannot be expected to affect sub-surface electrical activity in the heart wall.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation in the field.

claim: Ex vivo studies on small mammalian hearts consistently demonstrate the success of optogenetic defibrillation without providing a clear mechanism for the same.
source: However, ex vivo studies on small mammalian hearts consistently demonstrate the success of optogenetic defibrillation, without providing a clear mechanism for the same (Bruegmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited prior work.

claim: Some studies try to explain the mechanism behind the success of optogenetic defibrillation using the critical mass hypothesis.
source: Some studies try to explain the mechanism behind this success, using the critical mass hypothesis (Zipes et al., 1975).
evidence: This is a summary of approaches from cited prior work.

claim: According to the critical mass hypothesis, a spiral (scroll) wave requires a minimum area (volume) of excitable tissue for its sustainment.
source: According to this hypothesis, a spiral (scroll) wave requires a minimum area (volume) of excitable tissue for its sustainment.
evidence: This is a description of a hypothesis from cited prior work.

claim: By applying supra-threshold light to the surface of the epicardium, one can effectively reduce available area (volume) of excitable tissue to below the threshold requirement for spiral sustainability, thereby forcing the wavefront of the spiral (scroll) wave to collide with its waveback, resulting in its termination.
source: By applying supra-threshold light to the surface of the epicardium, one can effectively reduce available area (volume) of excitable tissue to below the threshold requirement for spiral sustainability, thereby forcing the wavefront of the spiral (scroll) wave to collide with its waveback, resulting in its termination.
evidence: This is a description of a mechanism from the critical mass hypothesis.

claim: The study postulates an alternative theory to the critical mass hypothesis for explaining successful optogenetic defibrillation.
source: However, our studies postulate an alternative theory.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the current study.

claim: The application of light to the epicardial surface effectively leads to a transmural illumination gradient within the heart wall, with both sub-threshold and supra-threshold illumination régimes.
source: We propose that the application of light to the epicardial surface effectively leads to a transmural illumination gradient within the heart wall, with both sub-threshold and supra-threshold illumination régimes.
evidence: This is a proposed theory from the current study.

claim: A linear gradient of pure sub-threshold illumination has the potential to induce a drift of a spiral wave into the region of higher illumination (i.e. the epicardial surface in a transmural section of the heart wall), thereby protecting the internal tissue from hidden electrical activity.
source: Our study shows that a linear gradient of pure sub-threshold illumination has the potential to induce a drift of a spiral wave into the region of higher illumination (i.e. the epicardial surface in a transmural section of the heart wall), thereby protecting the internal tissue from hidden electrical activity.
evidence: This is presented as a finding from the study with implications for the proposed theory.

claim: Once electrical activity is drawn out to the surface by the induced drift, it can be terminated using global supra-threshold illumination, which then ensures electrical synchronization.
source: Once such activity is drawn out to the surface by the induced drift, it can be terminated using global supra-threshold illumination, which then ensures electrical synchronization.
evidence: This is part of the proposed theory from the current study.

claim: The study provides new mechanistic insights into the theory of successful optogenetic defibrillation in animal hearts, where application of light to the surface produces a gradient of illumination within the heart wall.
